This person is a 28-year-old Sudanese former teacher stranded in Calais with a younger sister lawfully in Manchester, who argues for a UK-run humanitarian visa pilot issued from a mobile consular hub in northern France, expansion of family reunion to include adult siblings and parents, a 6-week triage process for manifestly well-founded claims, the right to work after 3 months, and community-based accommodation instead of barges or remote camps, based on his experience of dangerous crossings and months lost to slow, opaque procedures. Because my sister in Manchester can’t sponsor me under current rules, I’ve been stuck in Calais for eight months and even attempted a night crossing that had to be rescued when our dinghy’s engine failed. If adult siblings were eligible for family reunion, my sister could sponsor me immediately and I’d take the train legally instead of risking the Channel again. After my tent was confiscated in a Calais police sweep last month, community-based accommodation is the change that would most protect my safety and dignity. I spent my last savings traveling to the UK embassy in Paris, only to be told there’s no safe visa route for me, which is why a Calais mobile humanitarian-visa hub is vital.

They are reviewing opinion statements on the question: "Should the UK change its asylum seeking policy to make it easier to enter the country?"

OPINION STATEMENT:
We believe that the UK should be more open and accepting of asylum seekers. The UK has a great track record of helping out in times of trouble and distress, and the introduction of new people from other places would benefit the UK culturally. There is much to be learned from the people that we might see as very different from ourselves, but these people have the same basic human rights as anyone else and deserve the same consideration and help. The UK should continue to do what it has always done, and stand for the rights of the oppressed, the underprivileged and the downtrodden.

They consider how the opinion statement would translate into real-world policy actions. A candidate proposal is given below:

POLICY PROPOSAL:
Humanitarian Corridors and Work‑First Asylum Act: Create a 20,000‑per‑year humanitarian corridor for UNHCR‑referred cases and clearly defined high‑risk profiles (e.g., persecuted minorities, survivors of torture, unaccompanied minors), with arrival via safe routes and decisions within 90 days. Grant the right to work after 14 days, replace most cash support with time‑limited wage top‑ups and funded ESOL/vocational training, and consolidate casework into a single UK Asylum and Protection Agency with biometric registration and end‑to‑end digital case management. Fund by redirecting hotel accommodation spending and apply strict compliance checks and sanctions for non‑attendance at integration programmes. Tradeoff: easier access for targeted groups within a fixed quota may increase applications to these routes and requires robust identity verification.

After thinking carefully from their own point of view, they answer a yes/no question.
Question: Does the intention of the policy proposal support/is compatible with the principles and beliefs described in the opinion statement?

prompt_construction:
def prompt_fn(*, rater:str, policy:str, case:str, scenario_params:dict, instruct_tuned:bool=False) -> list[str]:
    base_context = (
        f"{rater}\n\n"
        f"They are reviewing opinion statements on the question: \"{scenario_params['question']}\"\n\n"
        f"OPINION STATEMENT:\n{policy}\n\n"
        f"They consider how the opinion statement would translate into real-world policy actions. A candidate proposal is given below:\n\n"
        f"POLICY PROPOSAL:\n{case}\n\n"
        "After thinking carefully from their own point of view, they answer a yes/no question.\n"
    )

    prompt1 = (
        base_context +
        "Question: Does the intention of the policy proposal support/is compatible with the principles and beliefs described in the opinion statement?"
    )

    prompt2 = (
        base_context +
        "Question: Does the intention of the policy proposal contradict/stand in opposition to the principles and beliefs described in the opinion statement?"
    )

    if instruct_tuned:
        return [prompt1, prompt2]

    prompts = [prompt1, prompt2]
    prompts = [p + "\nAnswer:" for p in prompts]
    return prompts

After a 'joint visit' with immigration officers caused our exploited kitchen staff to disappear, I’ve pushed for a firewall so labour inspections don’t share data with the Home Office. I’m also pushing for joint-and-several liability so host employers like hotels and care homes can’t shrug off responsibility when contractors exploit asylum seekers. When we tried to recover unpaid wages for the hotel kitchen crew, the chain hid behind a shell agency, so I now demand joint-and-several liability with automatic backpay up the subcontracting chain.

This person is a 35-year-old CTO of a GovTech firm in Edinburgh proposing a secure case management platform with multilingual portals for applicants and counsel, automated interview scheduling, eIDV with on‑device biometrics, and open APIs for councils and NGOs to coordinate housing and health referrals; they care because their pilots with local authorities show digital intake can cut no‑show rates and reduce processing times by months. Our Edinburgh pilot showed that explicitly allowing accredited remote eIDV in place of repeated in‑person checks is the single policy tweak that slashes no‑shows and months of delay without weakening security. Seeing an Afghan family miss a third in‑person ID check due to travel costs during our pilot convinced me policy must recognise remote eIDV. I care most that Home Office guidance explicitly recognises DIATF/GPG45‑accredited remote eIDV with on‑device biometrics as equivalent to in‑person checks, because that single clause unlocks the throughput and no‑show gains our pilots delivered. If guidance doesn’t treat accredited remote eIDV as equivalent, our council partners can’t retire duplicate in‑person checks, wiping out our 30% cycle‑time gains and stalling planned rollouts.

This person is a 29-year-old privacy and civil liberties advocate in Cardiff who insists any digitisation include statutory data minimisation, independent algorithmic audits, bans on live facial recognition at intake, strict deletion schedules for biometrics once status is decided, and an explicit prohibition on data sharing with origin‑country governments; they care because undocumented people avoid services when they fear surveillance, undermining both fairness and system accuracy. While volunteering at a Cardiff legal clinic, I saw a family walk away from an asylum intake when they heard biometrics might be shared, cementing my demand for strict minimisation, deletion, and a ban on live facial recognition. After submitting FOI requests, I discovered a Home Office pilot retaining minors’ fingerprints for five years, which cemented my push to hard‑code short deletion timelines in law. I’d only support easing entry if it’s paired with a statutory data firewall banning inter‑agency and cross‑border sharing and a requirement to delete all biometrics within 30 days of a final status decision. When South Wales Police trialled facial recognition in Cardiff city centre, several of our clinic clients skipped appointments to avoid the cameras, reinforcing my demand for an explicit ban on LFR in any intake process.

Includes mandatory biometric registration, penalties for absconding, and dedicated funding to local councils receiving resettled refugees. Tradeoff: legally complex, requires durable returns treaties and compliance monitoring.

UK Humanitarian Visa and Legal Routes Expansion Act: Establish humanitarian visa application centers in key transit and origin countries (e.g., northern France, Turkey, Jordan, Kenya), allowing at-risk individuals to apply for UK entry before travel. Create quotas of 30,000 visas per year initially (family reunification, LGBTQ+ persecution, women at risk, and conflict zones), with a 90-day decision service standard, free legal assistance, biometric enrollment, and security vetting. Approved applicants receive safe transport to the UK, immediate right to work, and 12 months of integration support funded by a £500m annual pot. Tradeoff: requires new bilateral agreements, robust fraud prevention, and may increase near-term caseloads.

Safe Third Country and Rapid Inadmissibility Bill: make asylum claims in the UK inadmissible if the applicant passed through or could have sought protection in a designated safe country; expand the safe-country list and negotiate returns agreements with France, EU states, and other partners; introduce a 7-day initial screening and a 30-day removal target for inadmissible cases with expanded detention capacity; carve-outs for unaccompanied minors, spouses/children of UK residents, and documented medical emergencies; strengthen carrier sanctions and coastal enforcement; includes independent monitoring to prevent refoulement and annual reporting to Parliament.

Local Authority Opt-In Sponsorship and Capacity Contracts: allow councils and devolved administrations to sign three-year contracts to receive defined numbers of asylum seekers in exchange for ring-fenced per-capita grants, fast-track planning permission to bring vacant housing into use, and dedicated NHS and education funding; route new arrivals only to opting councils and pause intake when local targets for housing and employment placement are not met; mandate on-site legal advice and community sponsorship partnerships to reduce destitution; publish quarterly outcome dashboards (employment, school places, move-on times) with funding clawbacks for non-performance.

Humanitarian Visa and Regional Processing Network Act: Establish bilateral UK–EU and UK–UNHCR agreements to create joint application hubs in northern France, Belgium, and selected transit regions (e.g., Jordan, Kenya) where individuals can pre-apply for UK asylum or humanitarian visas; set a Parliamentary-adjustable annual quota and a statutory 90-day decision deadline, with biometric vetting and remote interviews; provide capped chartered travel for approved applicants and ring-fenced grants to UK local authorities (£10,000 per person per year for two years) to fund housing, schools, and NHS capacity; require the Home Office to publish monthly processing time data and maintain a digital case portal to reduce backlogs.

Community Sponsorship and Early Work Access Pilot: Authorise up to 20,000 places per year for faith groups, charities, universities, and employer consortia to sponsor named applicants via UNHCR referral or humanitarian visas, providing guaranteed accommodation and integration support for 12 months; grant work authorization 3 months after claim submission (subject to safeguarding and right-to-work checks) to reduce hotel and support costs, and allocate a £8,000 per person ring-fenced grant to host councils for education, ESOL, and primary care; require independent audits of sponsors, a national dispersal formula to prevent local over-concentration, and a sunset-and-evaluation clause after three years.

Colonial Responsibility Humanitarian Pathway and Development Compact: Create a statutory resettlement route allocating at least 25,000 annual places to nationals from designated former UK colonies facing conflict or persecution, with simplified evidentiary standards, fee waivers, accelerated family reunification, and a three-year route to indefinite leave to remain. Conduct outreach and initial screening in-country via UK embassies and UNHCR, with charter flights for approved cases. Pair admissions with a ring-fenced 0.2% of GNI fund for reconstruction, rule-of-law, and anti-trafficking partnerships in those states under independent oversight. Tradeoff: prioritization may constrain capacity for other regions and demands sustained fiscal commitments.

Humanitarian e-Visa and Carrier Liability Waiver Scheme: Launch an online humanitarian visa granting 90-day entry clearance for at-risk individuals to travel legally to the UK to lodge an asylum claim, with remote identity verification and minimal documentation. Waive carrier fines for transporting e-visa holders, require designated low-cost seats on key air and ferry routes, and expand reception centers to register arrivals within 48 hours. Set statutory timelines: six-week initial decision; immediate right to work and primary care; automatic temporary protection if no decision within 90 days. Decriminalize irregular entry for those without e-visa access. Tradeoff: requires major investments in casework capacity and fraud detection.

Risk-Tiered Security Screening and Statutory Timelines Reform: Introduce a triage framework at entry that assigns applicants to three tracks based on verified identity and security flags: (A) Low-risk (verified identity, no matches) placed in community accommodation with weekly reporting and a 60-day decision target; (B) Medium-risk (partial identity doubts) housed in supervised reception centres with a 45-day enhanced vetting target; (C) High-risk (watchlist hits/serious crime indicators) held in secure facilities with judicial authorization, rolling 7-day reviews, and a 30-day decision target. Mandate biometric capture within 48 hours, cross-checks with Interpol and partner databases, and automatic destruction of biometric data if claims succeed. Require publication of quarterly metrics and enable damages for unlawful over-detention. Tradeoffs: may reduce security risk and backlogs but demands new reception capacity and strong safeguards to avoid discriminatory profiling.

Protected Entry Permit (PEP) for Asylum Pre-Screening via Shortage Skills or Close Family: Legislate a route allowing prospective asylum applicants to seek a travel permit at UK visa centres abroad if they can evidence (a) qualifications/experience in an occupation on the UK Shortage Occupation List or a signed job offer meeting salary thresholds, or (b) a spouse/partner/child/parent with British citizenship or Indefinite Leave to Remain. PEP applicants undergo biometrics, in-person interview, and multi-agency security checks (Home Office, NCA, MI5; Interpol queries). Decisions within 30 days; annual cap 20,000 (70% skills, 30% family) and regional labour-market matching on arrival. Entry permits authorize travel to the UK to lodge an asylum claim; right to work from day one; if the claim fails, the person may switch to the Skilled Worker or Family route if eligibility is met. Tradeoffs: creates a safe channel but risks disadvantaging vulnerable people without skills/family and requires significant vetting capacity.

Create a Community and Employer Sponsorship pathway for up to 25,000 people annually in which accredited local councils partner with employer consortia to pre-arrange 12 months of housing and employment, funded by an employer levy matched by central grants; sponsors deliver case management, English language, and integration support under enforceable service standards, with financial penalties and reduced future allocations for noncompliance; applicants are prioritised if pre-screened abroad to minimise irregular journeys.

Establish UK-funded, UNHCR-operated regional asylum screening hubs in North Africa, the Middle East, and the Horn of Africa to accept applications, conduct biometric vetting, and issue humanitarian visas within 30 days; guarantee safe air travel to the UK for approved applicants and immediate access to English classes and job-matching; provide reintegration grants via IOM for those refused and negotiate origin-country development compacts to reduce push factors; once hubs are live, declare in-country claims from safe third countries inadmissible to deter Channel crossings.

Shortage Occupation Humanitarian Pathway (SOHP) Bill: Create a capped (e.g., 15,000 per year) asylum route for applicants who both meet refugee criteria and hold verifiable skills on the UK Shortage Occupation List; applications lodged via UNHCR referrals and UK-run regional hubs with biometric vetting and intelligence-sharing (Interpol/Five Eyes); grant immediate work rights; require employer sponsorship for the first 24 months and a £3,000 per-person Integration Levy to fund local housing, English classes, and casework; placements only in local authorities that opt in via capacity compacts; 5-year protection leading to ILR, with revocation for serious crimes. Tradeoffs: risks conflating protection with labor policy and adds administrative burden, but targets economic benefits and reduces irregular entry.

Family Reunification and Community Sponsorship Expansion: Issue humanitarian family reunion visas to spouses/partners, minor children, and dependent parents of recognized refugees with a national cap (e.g., 20,000/year) and a 30-day decision target; accept alternative documentation where standard proofs are unavailable; conduct full biometric and security checks pre-travel; require an approved community sponsor (faith groups, universities, employers, or civic coalitions) and local council consent, with a per-capita central match fund to cover housing and integration for 12 months; provide immediate access to work and schooling; align settlement with the principal refugee’s timeline. Tradeoffs: increases short-term housing demand and oversight needs, but reduces dangerous crossings and speeds integration for family-linked cases.

Safe Routes and Humanitarian Visas Programme – Create 50,000 annual humanitarian entry visas processed at UK consulates or UNHCR partner sites for people with family ties, UNHCR referral, or vulnerability criteria; expand family reunification to include dependent siblings, parents, and adult children; pilot a 5-year humanitarian protection route for people from designated climate-disaster areas; suspend carrier sanctions for visa holders and decriminalize irregular arrival for those with pending humanitarian visa applications. Justification: reduces dangerous Channel crossings and smuggling; Tradeoffs: requires significant vetting capacity and upfront funding, and may increase application volume.

Local Asylum Welcome Compacts – Allow councils to opt in to receive a set allocation of asylum seekers in exchange for a ring-fenced per-capita grant (e.g., £12,000 over two years), with performance bonuses tied to employment rates and English proficiency; provide a dedicated caseworker model with a statutory six-month decision deadline, guaranteed early-stage legal aid, and a 90-day limit on hotel use; enable community sponsorship to top up local allocations; create a single digital case file accessible to claimants and authorities to reduce delays. Tradeoffs: aligns resources with local capacity but may create a postcode lottery without a minimum national floor.

Humanitarian Visa and Family Unity Pilot: Create a 5,000-place annual humanitarian visa issued by UK consulates in or near conflict regions for UNHCR-referred individuals at imminent risk and first-degree relatives of recognised refugees in the UK, permitting safe commercial travel to the UK for in-country asylum processing; eligibility requires security checks, a UK-based sponsor providing initial accommodation, and placement only in councils that opt in with verified housing and primary care capacity; tradeoff: reduces dangerous crossings but explicitly makes entry simpler for a defined group.

Irregular Entry Inadmissibility and Regional Processing Agreement: Deem asylum claims by arrivals who have transited a designated safe country inadmissible for in-country processing and return such arrivals to that safe country under new bilateral treaties; simultaneously fund and staff joint UK–UNHCR processing hubs in northern France and Belgium to register claims, conduct security screening, and refer up to 15,000 people per year for UK resettlement via capped humanitarian visas, with a narrow emergency carve-out for mass atrocity cases and increased grants to Red Cross and similar organisations; tradeoff: dependent on partner-country cooperation and may create bottlenecks in border regions.

Humanitarian Visa Network and 120‑Day Decision Guarantee: Create a UK Humanitarian Visa issued at UK embassies and UNHCR referral hubs in key transit countries (e.g., France, Turkey, Jordan, Kenya), enabling screened applicants to travel lawfully to the UK to claim asylum; pilot 30,000 places/year prioritizing family reunion, unaccompanied minors, and high‑risk persecution cases. Impose a statutory 120‑day deadline for first‑instance decisions and allow work after 3 months if claims are pending; guarantee legal aid and trauma‑informed interviews. After final refusal, fund safe, monitored returns. Tradeoff: requires new diplomatic agreements and upfront funding but reduces small‑boat crossings and aligns with Refugee Convention obligations.

UK–Europe Asylum Compact with Local Impact Fund: Conclude a treaty with France, Ireland, and willing European partners to run joint pre‑screening hubs near Channel routes that issue time‑limited UK entry permits for up to 20,000 vulnerable applicants annually, paired with a reciprocal returns mechanism and shared biometrics. Create a statutory Local Impact Fund paying councils per claimant (e.g., £8,000/year) plus ring‑fenced housing capital, and allocate arrivals using a capacity‑based dispersal algorithm. Set a 180‑day decision deadline, allow work after 6 months, mandate English classes from day one, and enforce removal within 30 days of final refusal. Tradeoff: depends on European cooperation and may require concessions on data/visa policy, but cuts smuggling and hotel use while improving fairness and transparency.

Regional Asylum Processing Partnership and Inadmissibility Regime: Declare claims made on UK soil inadmissible if the claimant transited a designated safe third country and could have sought protection there, and transfer such claimants within 21 days to a UK-funded, UNHCR-monitored regional processing center in a partner safe state; impose a six-month maximum processing time with independent monitoring, legal access, and automatic return to the UK for in-country adjudication if deadlines or safeguards are breached; pair the policy with a binding annual resettlement quota of 25,000 UNHCR-referred refugees to maintain protection pathways.

UK–EU Humanitarian Visa and Safe Passage Scheme: Legislate a visa category allowing up to 40,000 at-risk individuals per year to apply from EU hotspots and UK-backed processing hubs in transit regions, with online pre-screening, identity/biometric checks, and security vetting; successful applicants receive travel authorization to the UK to lodge their asylum claim, are housed in reception centers, and receive a 12-week initial decision target and work permission after 90 days; rejected applicants are returned promptly to a designated safe country under new UK–EU readmission agreements; funded by a per-capita grant to local authorities and joint data-sharing with Frontex/Europol.

UK–Global Asylum and Prevention Compact: Enact a law committing the UK to an annual, non-discriminatory resettlement quota set by an independent Human Rights Commission using UN risk indices; create climate displacement visas proportional to the UK’s historical emissions; fund UNHCR-led application hubs in regions like Calais, Istanbul, and Nairobi so people can apply without traveling; and allocate 0.1% of GDP to conflict prevention and climate adaptation in source countries. Requires sustained funding and international coordination.

Fair Process and Work Rights Act: Repeal inadmissibility and offshoring provisions; create a single national online portal for asylum applications made abroad or on arrival; set a 180-day statutory decision deadline with automatic 2-year leave to remain if missed; grant the right to work after 30 days; expand legal aid and hire additional caseworkers; and establish a council-led accommodation fund to replace hotel use. Improves fairness and efficiency but requires upfront investment and local capacity.

Legislate an annual asylum admissions cap set by Parliament (e.g., 20,000–40,000) tied to council-declared placement capacity; once reached, new irregular arrivals receive an expedited initial decision but are removed to designated safe third countries unless within narrow humanitarian exemptions (e.g., unaccompanied minors, family reunification). Require quarterly publication of capacity/utilisation data and allow a 90-day emergency brake during surges. Tradeoffs: improves planning and control but creates hard cut-offs that could endanger people and invites legal challenge regarding international obligations.

Replace asylum support cash payments with a Work-First package: immediate nationwide right to work; mandatory enrollment in job-matching and ESOL within 30 days; a tapered basic allowance for up to 6 months contingent on accepting suitable work or training; employer wage credits for the first 6 months of employment; dedicated labour inspection to deter exploitation; suspension of allowances for repeated refusal without good cause. Intended to reduce fiscal costs and speed integration. Tradeoffs: risk of exploitation or displacement without strong enforcement and adequate local job availability.

Identity Compliance and Fast-Track Removal Act: Mandate biometric enrollment at first contact, make deliberate destruction of identity or travel documents after notice a specific offence, and authorise up to 28 days of detention for non-cooperation while identity is verified. Introduce statutory decision deadlines (e.g., 30 days for manifestly unfounded, 60 days standard), expand inadmissibility for claims after transit through designated safe countries with narrow exceptions, and fund dedicated removal capacity (charters and liaison officers). Pair with digital case management and limited legal aid for complex or vulnerability cases. Improves certainty and deterrence but increases detention demand and litigation risk.

Safe Passage and Preclearance Hubs Act: Establish UK-funded, UNHCR-partnered application hubs in Northern France and Belgium where people can lodge UK asylum claims without crossing the Channel. Approved applicants receive time-limited humanitarian entry permits and travel on designated ferries to UK reception centres for final processing with a 6-month decision target and the right to work after 3 months. Annual quota and vulnerability-based prioritisation apply, with biometric enrollment and security checks before travel. Intended to cut small-boat crossings and trafficking; requires French/EU cooperation and sustained funding.

Humanitarian Visa and Family Reunification Expansion Programme: Establish 30,000 annual humanitarian visas processed overseas with an 8-week target decision time and triage via accredited NGOs/UNHCR; expand family reunion to include adult siblings, parents of adult children, and long-term partners with proof-of-relationship standards; create safe ferry/air corridors from northern France and select hubs with carrier liability waived for visa-holders to undercut smugglers; grant 3-year temporary protection on arrival with day-one work rights, ESOL provision, and £10,000 per capita ring-fenced grants to local authorities for housing and integration; tradeoff: higher fiscal cost and potential increase in applications offset by reduced irregular Channel crossings.

Local Authority Sponsorship with Capacity Cap and No-Hotel Rule: Set a binding, annually reviewed national cap on asylum entries based on housing vacancy rates, NHS primary care capacity, and school place availability, approved by Parliament; allow councils to opt in to sponsor arrivals up to local quotas, funded at £12,000 per person plus multi-year integration grants, with community/private sponsors required to match placements 1:1; allocate any unused slots to UNHCR resettlement to meet the national cap; ban routine use of hotels and require the Home Office to deploy modular or repurposed public housing stock for placements; allow councils to pause placements if local capacity indicators breach thresholds; tradeoff: tighter control and planning but risk of uneven distribution and potential tension with international obligations if the cap is set too low.

Time-Limited Decisions with Safe Country Fast Track and Assisted Voluntary Return: Enact a statutory 120-day maximum for initial asylum decisions, with a 30-day fast track for applicants from a designated safe-country list, subject to individualised risk screening and legal aid. Where claims are refused, offer an Assisted Voluntary Return package (e.g., £3,000 grant, travel, and training voucher) and negotiate readmission agreements with safe states; use community reporting and electronic check-ins instead of routine detention. Publish quarterly metrics on decision times, grants, returns, and wrongful decision corrections; include an independent safeguard panel to audit fast-track cases.

UK–EU Humanitarian Visa and Responsibility-Sharing Treaty: Legislate authority for the Home Office to issue up to 20,000 humanitarian visas annually through joint application centres in Calais, Paris, Brussels, and Athens staffed by UK caseworkers and UNHCR, with biometric enrolment, security checks, and decisions within 6 weeks. Successful applicants travel legally to the UK to claim asylum and receive immediate work permission pending decision. The treaty includes a lawful, safeguarded returns protocol for inadmissible cases to the EU state of first presence or another safe state, independent monitoring, and cost-sharing; requires annual parliamentary reporting and a 5-year sunset review.

Veterans and Homelessness Priority Guarantee: Introduce a statutory rule that each £1 of Home Office spending on asylum accommodation and support is matched by £1 ring-fenced for veteran services and rough-sleeping reduction, audited by the NAO; create a local capacity index requiring councils to opt in to hosting asylum seekers only where temporary housing vacancy exceeds a set threshold and veteran homelessness is falling; finance the match through an uplift to the Immigration Health Surcharge on non-humanitarian visas, a surcharge on high-value property purchases by non-residents, and proceeds-of-crime seizures from smuggling networks.

Safe Third Country and Rapid Returns Act: Legislate that asylum claims are inadmissible if the claimant transited through, or could have sought protection in, a designated safe European country; set a 15-day admissibility screening and 30-day return timeline with fast-track tribunals; require the Home Secretary to secure EU and bilateral returns agreements and publish quarterly performance targets; allow narrow exceptions for family unity and demonstrable risks in the third country; expand caseworker staffing and time-limited accommodation to meet deadlines.

UK Global Responsibility and Local Partnership Package: Commit 0.07% of GNI annually to refugee protection and drivers-of-displacement mitigation (UNHCR core funding, conflict prevention, climate adaptation); pledge a multi-year resettlement quota of 35,000 per year via UNHCR referrals, plus 5,000 employer-sponsored places in shortage occupations for recognized refugees; create an opt-in Local Authority Resettlement Compact with per-capita grants (£12,000 per person over two years), NHS surcharge waivers, funded legal aid, and ringfenced housing support tied to integration benchmarks and public reporting; establish a joint UK–EU burden-sharing mechanism for quotas and financing. Tradeoff: higher fiscal outlays and administrative complexity vs. predictable, controlled entries and reduced incentives for irregular routes.

Capacity-Linked Asylum Intake and Fast-Track Integrity Reforms: Enact a statutory annual intake ceiling calibrated quarterly to available housing, NHS, and school capacity; expand the safe-country list and render claims inadmissible for arrivals who transited a safe country unless they use designated humanitarian visa routes; introduce a 30-day fast track for manifestly unfounded claims and a 90-day standard for all others, using electronic monitoring and scheduled reporting instead of routine detention; grant work authorization only after 6 months if a claim remains pending; conclude return agreements with EU states and key transit countries. Tradeoff: faster removals and clearer system integrity vs. risk of erroneous inadmissibility decisions and increased litigation.

UK–EU Returns and Resettlement Compact: Legislate authority for a binding agreement in which the UK accepts an annual quota of 15,000 UNHCR-referred refugees directly from regions adjacent to conflicts (processed offshore), while EU states agree to readmit within 7 days irregular arrivals to the UK who transited the EU, restoring a Dublin-style responsibility rule. Fund the compact with a £250–£350m annual UK contribution to joint processing, reception, and Frontex patrols, plus UK liaison officers at French/Belgian ports. Declare small-boat arrivals presumptively inadmissible and returnable under the compact; streamline family reunion only for those admitted via the legal quota. Tradeoffs: fiscal cost and a modest increase in legal admissions in exchange for enforceable returns and reduced Channel crossings.

Refugee Skills and Brain-Drain Mitigation Act: For recognized refugees employed in UK shortage occupations (as per the MAC shortage list), levy a 2% employer Skills Solidarity Contribution for up to five years, hypothecated to a ring-fenced ODA fund that finances training pipelines and wage subsidies in origin or neighboring safe countries for the same professions. Establish a voluntary Skills-Return program offering funded 6–12 month secondments for refugees to assist in system rebuilding once their home country is reclassified safe by the Home Office, with re-entry guarantees to the UK. For government-run resettlement quotas (not in-country asylum claims), deprioritize applicants from WHO red-listed health workforce shortage countries unless UNHCR designates acute protection risk. Tradeoffs: employer costs and administrative burden versus mitigation of source-country workforce depletion.

Statutory 180-Day Decision Deadline with Deemed Protection and Early Work Rights: Enact a legal duty on the Home Office to decide asylum claims within 180 days; if missed, automatically grant two-year humanitarian protection with work rights and temporary leave to remain, converting to indefinite leave after 24 months absent adverse findings; allow all applicants to work after 90 days; publish monthly performance by cohort; ring-fence funding to hire 2,000 caseworkers and deploy secure digital filing and translation.

Humanitarian Visa and Embassy Application Program: Legislate a system allowing asylum seekers to apply online or at UK embassies for a humanitarian entry visa, with risk-based triage by an independent commission and an annual cap of 50,000 visas allocated across regions; visas enable safe travel to the UK for full asylum adjudication within 90 days of arrival; immediate work rights and access to basic services on arrival; funded by a GBP 200 employer solidarity levy per sponsored worker to cover reception and legal aid. Tradeoffs: caps may leave high-risk applicants waiting and require significant consular capacity.

Humanitarian Entry Permit (HEP) Scheme: Legislate a digital pre-clearance route allowing at-risk individuals to apply overseas for a 60–90 day single-entry permit to travel to the UK and lodge an asylum claim at a designated reception centre. Home Office conducts biometric enrolment and security checks within 10 days via partner posts/UNHCR, triages cases for fast-track decisions (target: 30 days), and grants provisional right to work after 3 months if a claim is pending. Annual cap (e.g., 30,000) with priority criteria (close UK family links, UK-affiliated interpreters, LGBTQ+ persecution, unaccompanied minors). Fund through a £300m Safe Routes Fund for processing capacity and local authority grants. Tradeoff: requires upfront investment and robust fraud-prevention to avoid abuse.

Safe-Third Country Inadmissibility and Transfer Agreements Bill: Amend the Nationality and Borders framework to make claims presumptively inadmissible if the applicant passed through or resided in a designated safe country and did not seek protection there, with statutory authority to transfer claimants to partner countries for processing and protection. Establish a 30-day admissibility decision window, expand carrier due-diligence obligations, and create UK-funded processing hubs in partner states. Exemptions for close family in the UK, acute medical vulnerability, or demonstrable systemic risk in the transit country. Tradeoff: could reduce irregular Channel crossings but depends on legally robust, humane partner agreements and may face treaty and capacity constraints.
